title.narrative: TRANSFORM Soil Fertility management in Ethiopia

description.narrative: Ethiopia has implemented a range of initiatives to enhance agricultural productivity, including providing small-scale farmers with fertilizers, high-quality seeds, and training in improved farming techniques. However, soil health continues to decline, with widespread issues such as acidity, salinity, nutrient depletion, low organic matter, and erosion, signs of persistent land degradation that threaten the sustainability of agriculture. This deterioration not only reduces crop yields but also endangers the livelihoods of millions of farmers who rely on agriculture as their primary source of income. To address the productivity gap while conserving and restoring soil health, the TRANSFORM Program aims to actively engage small-scale farmers in the solutions. TRANSFORM will be implemented over four years, from 2025 to 2028, across three regions: Oromia, Amhara, and Central Ethiopia.TRANSFORM is structured around four key components: (i) customizing soil fertility extension services to empower farmer households and communities, (ii) building a vibrant sector for soil inputs to ensure that farmers have access to essential resources, (iii) strengthening linkages between research and extension through bottom-up, participatory farmer-led action research, which promotes innovative solutions tailored to local contexts, and (iv) fostering an enabling environment for soil health and fertility to encourage collaborative efforts among stakeholders. The Program is implemented by a consortium of partners, including the IFDC as the lead partner, along with Stichting Wageningen Research (SWR) - Wageningen Environmental Research (WENR), ISRIC – World Soil Information, the Environment and Coffee Forest Forum (ECFF), and SOS Sahel (Ethiopia) as the implementing partners. Together, these partners are committed to establishing sustainable soil health and fertility management practices to support a resilient agricultural landscape in Ethiopia.

General objective:- to see 65,000 ha of farmland converted to sustainable land use. - to enhance 100,000 small-scale food producers and their agro-ecological farmlands become more resilient to shocks- to achieve systemic uplift and transformation of local and multi-sectoral actors with strengthened knowledge and implementation capacity for soil fertility and health.Specific objectives:- to resile and empower small-scale farmers and communities to become stewards of their soils.- to establish a vibrant and functional soil input system through private sector- to implement inclusive, bottom-up, participatory approaches to soil health and fertility management - to adopt an integrated and holistic approach for coordinating soil health and fertility management.Expected Outcomes- Empowered Households: the integration of sustainable soil health and fertility management improves soil and crop productivity, increases household incomes, enhances food security, provides better livelihoods, and promotes sustainable use of soil resources.- Restored Farmlands: implementing integrated land management practices enhances soil health, increases biodiversity, and improves water management, ultimately resulting in more sustainable agricultural systems and greater resilience to climate change.- Enhanced Community Knowledge: The enhanced knowledge and skills of local communities and multi-sectoral actors in sustainable soil health management promote the adoption of sustainable soil health and fertility practices, increase resilience to environmental and economic challenges, and foster a brighter future for generations to come.Expected outputs:- Sustainable soil health and fertility management practices integrated and empowered 100,000 households, with 30% participation from women and 30% from youth.- Integrated land management practices implemented across 128 kebeles and 128 watersheds and sustainably restored 65,000 hectares of farmland.- Capacity (knowledge and skills) of local and multi-sectoral actors for implementing sustainable soil fertility and health practices enhanced through targeted training, practical demonstrations, and partnerships, leading to improved agricultural productivity and community resilience.- National and regional soil health and fertility platforms established and institutionalized that integrate a holistic approach, fostering coordination and alignment among soil actors and stakeholders at all levels and creating an enabling environment for informed policy decisions.

recipient-country.narrative: The program is entirely implemented in Ethiopia.

description.narrative: The total contribution for the 4 years (December 31,2028）

title.narrative: 2.Small scale food producers and their agro-ecological farmlands become more resilient to shocks
2.1Hectares of agricultural land that agro-ecologically became more resilient to shocks

description.narrative: Agricultural land that has improved its capacity to withstand and recover from environmental and climate-related stresses, such as droughts, floods, and soil degradation. This resilience is defined by factors such as enhanced soil health through ISFM, soil and water conservation measures (e.g., terracing, rainwater harvesting, trench), diversified cropping systems (e.g., intercropping, agroforestry), use of drought-resistant crops, conservation agriculture, in-situ water conservation, upstream watershed management, supplementary irrigation, and reduced dependence on external synthetic inputs. These practices contribute to sustainable productivity, ecosystem stability, and long-term food security.

comment.narrative: An impact-level indicator, measurement is not expected during the first year, as changes at this level require a longer time frame to materialize.

title.narrative: 2.2Small-scale food producers whose livelihood became more resilient to shocks

description.narrative: Small-scale food producers who have strengthened their ability to withstand and recover from climate, economic, and environmental challenges. This resilience is achieved through diversified farming systems, improved soil and water management, access to climate-adaptive seeds and soil inputs, sustainable agroecological practices, and better market access. These measures enhance food security (e.g. percentage of households moved from sever food insecurity to moderate and food secure), household food insecurity access scale (HFIAS), income stability (income diversification index with score of income sources), and long-term sustainability, reducing vulnerability to droughts (percentage decrease in recovery time after shock), price fluctuations, and other shocks.

comment.narrative: An impact-level indicator, measurement is not expected during the first year, as changes at this level require a longer time frame to materialize.

title.narrative: Outcome 4: Integrated and holistic approach of stakeholders to coordinate soil health and fertility management initiatives at all levels.
4.115-year vision developed for soil health and fertility.

description.narrative: A comprehensive, national vision document outlining national goals, priorities, pathways and actions for sustainable soil health and fertility management over a 15-year period, developed through inclusive stakeholder consultation.

comment.narrative: There was no such document being implemented at the time of baseline. However, the government of Ethiopia has been developing 10-year road map for fertilizer and soil health.
It is not planned in 2025 as it was mainly an inception period.

The team has reviewed the 10-year fertilizer and soil health road map launched by the Ethiopian Ministry of Agriculture and preparing to contribute to its implementation instead of developing new vision document.

title.narrative: 4.2. Functional biofertilizer registration and labelling system.

description.narrative: An operational, government-endorsed system with clear procedures, standards, and guidelines for registering, testing, approving, and labelling of biofertilizer products to ensure quality, safety, and transparency in the market.

comment.narrative: In 2025, only preparatory activities were implemented toward the development of a functional biofertilizer registration and labelling system. These efforts focused on collaboration with government authorities to establish biofertilizer standards and to strengthen the capacity of regulatory institutions for registration processes and guideline development.

title.narrative: Outcome 2: Vibrant and functional Soil input system through private sector engagement
2.1Number of small-scale entrepreneurs involved in small scale production of soil inputs

description.narrative: Number of small-scale entrepreneurs including cooperative enterprises involved in production and distribution of soil inputs like compost, vermicompost, biochar, biofertilizers, organic fertilizers etc.

comment.narrative: In 2025, the intervention focused on identifying potential small-scale entrepreneurs and providing capacity building technical training on the production and application of organic soil inputs. Entrepreneurs demonstrating promising progress and a willingness to co invest in the business will be formalized, and additional technical support will be provided in 2026.

title.narrative: 2.2Quantity (MT) of lime supplied to small-scale producers in selected woredas.

description.narrative: Quantity of agricultural lime (metric ton) supplied and used for acid soil management.

comment.narrative: In 2025, an assessment was conducted to identify gaps in the agricultural lime supply chain. Based on the findings of this assessment, a last mile distribution plan will be developed in 2026 to improve coordination and ensure an efficient and effective supply chain.

title.narrative: 3.Systemic uplift and transformation of local and multisectoral actors with strengthened knowledge and implementation capacity for soil fertility and health
3.2Number of actions/measures/activities implemented in line with the 15-year vision developed for soil health and fertility

description.narrative: The indicator counts the total number of concrete actions, measures, or activities—such as policies enacted, training sessions delivered, demonstration sites established, or conservation practices adopted—that are implemented in alignment with the priorities and targets set out in the 15-year national vision for soil health and fertility.

comment.narrative: An impact-level indicator, measurement is not expected during the first year, as changes at this level require a longer time frame to materialize.

title.narrative: 3.1Number of public sector actors with increased capacity to effectively implement soil health and fertility initiatives/policies

description.narrative: The number of multisectoral actors who have demonstrated improved knowledge, skills, and mobilize resources to develop, promote, and enforce sustainable soil health and fertility management practices. This includes manuals, guidelines, directives, regulations and policies) developed, workshops organized, and number of training courses conducted.

comment.narrative: An impact-level indicator, measurement is not expected during the first year, as changes at this level require a longer time frame to materialize.

title.narrative: Output 1.1.Participatory, bottom-up and (gender) inclusive extension services
1.1.1 Number of DAs and extension staff capacitated in participatory extension approaches and ISFM techniques (directly reached)

description.narrative: The number of DAs and extension staff who have successfully completed training to improve their knowledge and skills in participatory extension methods and Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM) practices.

comment.narrative: The program trained 227 development agents （25% women and 67% youth in participatory extension and Integrated Soil Fertility Management （ISFM), reaching 23% of the overall target. This rollout has successfully established the institutional foundation for scaling the participatory integrated farm planning approach across the program's target areas.

title.narrative: 1.1.2 Number of TVET teachers capacitated in inclusive, bottom-up, participatory extension approaches, soil health and fertility practices, and data use, collection, and management

description.narrative: The number of TVET instructors who have received targeted training to teach inclusive, participatory extension methods, sustainable soil management practices, and effective data handling techniques.

comment.narrative: In 2025, a curriculum review was planned and progressed well during the reporting year; however, no capacity building training activities were planned during this period.

title.narrative: 1.1.3 Number of TVET students capacitated in inclusive, bottom-up, participatory extension approaches, soil health and fertility practices, and data use, collection, and management

description.narrative: The number of TVET students who have completed training modules or practical sessions that build their capacity in participatory extension, sustainable soil health practices, and accurate data management for agricultural development.

comment.narrative: In 2025, a curriculum review was planned and progressed well during the reporting year; however, no capacity building training activities were planned during this period.

title.narrative: Output 3.1Participatory farmer-led action research based on the needs of small-scale food producers
3.1.5DAs trained on using the Decision Support Tool for ISFM and fertilizers (as part of the pilot)

description.narrative: The number of Development Agents (DAs) who have received training on using a Decision Support Tool designed to improve planning and application of Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM) and fertilizer recommendations in pilot areas.

comment.narrative: No training on the Decision Support Tool (DST) was planned for 2025. However, DST calibration and other preparatory work were conducted during the reporting period. Training is planned for 2026, following the completion and finalization of the DST calibration.

title.narrative: 3.1.4MSc students and PhD students conducting evidence-based learning for different project related subjects

description.narrative: The number of enrolled MSc and PhD students whose thesis or research work directly contributes evidence-based insights relevant to project soil health and fertility objectives.

comment.narrative: The program supported four PhD and three MSc students to undertake research aligned with the program’s learning priorities and action research agenda.

title.narrative: 3.1.2Number of pilot kebeles where experiments are implemented with a diversity of soil inputs

description.narrative: The number of kebeles selected as pilot sites where farmers and partners implement and evaluate trials using multiple soil input types to identify best-fit practices.

comment.narrative: No experiments in pilot kebeles were planned under this indicator for 2025; however, preparatory steps were undertaken, including the selection of pilot kebeles and the development of farmer led action research agendas based on identified needs.

title.narrative: 3.1.3Number of researchers and government staff capacitated on inclusive, bottom-up, participatory scientific-led research in soil health and fertility (Disaggregated by Gender)

description.narrative: The number of researchers and government staff trained to design and implement inclusive, participatory research approaches that address farmer-prioritized soil health and fertility challenges, with gender-disaggregated reporting.

comment.narrative: During the reporting period, 104 researchers and government staff were trained, of whom 18% were women. The training focused on the Participatory Integrated Planning (PIP) approach, Participatory Action Research, and the CASCAPE three plots validation protocol, aimed at strengthening technical and facilitation capacities for field implementation.

title.narrative: 3.1.1Number of trials conducted by farmers, EIAR, selected RAIRIs and MoA.

description.narrative: The total number of on-farm and institutional trials carried out collaboratively by farmers, the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR), Regional Agricultural Research Institutes (RAIRIs), and the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) to test soil health and fertility practices.

comment.narrative: In 2025, farmers’ challenges were identified, and the corresponding action research agendas were validated for implementation in 2026.

title.narrative: Output 2.2Small-scale producers access and use soil inputs and services to contribute to restoration and conservation of soil health
2.2.3Online directory developed for soil input manufacturers and existing agro dealers and one-stop shops in the focus zones

description.narrative: A digital, publicly accessible directory listing verified soil input manufacturers, agro-dealers, and one-stop shops operating in designated focus zones to improve market transparency and farmer access.

comment.narrative: No online directory at the time of the baseline data collection.
Preparatory activities have been planned for the development of the online directory.
Mapping of existing manufacturers and distributors such as cooperatives, agro-dealers, and one-stop shops is conducted as preparation for development of directory in 2026.

title.narrative: 2.2.1Number of agro-dealers and primary cooperatives capacitated in knowledge on sustainable and appropriate soil input use

description.narrative: The number of agro-dealers and primary cooperatives whose representatives have received targeted training to improve their knowledge of sustainable, appropriate, and climate-smart soil input use.

comment.narrative: In 2025, existing agro-dealers and primary cooperatives were identified, and a preliminary needs assessment was conducted. Based on these findings, targeted capacity building activities are planned for implementation in 2026.

title.narrative: 2.2.2Number of small-scale producers using at least two soil inputs on their farms (gender disaggregated)

description.narrative: The number of small-scale producers who have adopted and applied at least two different types of soil inputs such as compost, lime, biofertilizers on their farms, reported with gender disaggregation.

comment.narrative: Capacity building activities reached 240 farmers and potential entrepreneurs, focusing on organic fertilizer production technologies, business modelling, and the regulatory framework for enterprise development. As a result, participants gained foundational knowledge of soil input production methods, enterprise options, and business formalization requirements. High performing small scale entrepreneurs received advanced hands on training and participated in exposure visits to research centres specializing in compost and vermicompost production. These efforts have led to the initiation of local organic fertilizer production and utilization. Scaling up production and systematically reporting on farmers adopting soil inputs will begin in 2026.

title.narrative: Output 4.3Variety of soil inputs registered for import and distribution
4.3.2Number of fertilizer products available in the market

description.narrative: The number of different fertilizer products actually stocked and sold in the market - available to farmers through licensed distributors, agro-dealers, cooperatives, and retail channels.

comment.narrative: Reporting on the number of fertilizer products available in the market is expected to begin in 2026, following the operationalization of soil input business cases.

title.narrative: 4.3.1Number of fertilizer products registered by the private sector.

description.narrative: The number of distinct fertilizer products that private sector companies have officially registered with national authorities for legal production, import, or distribution in Ethiopia.

comment.narrative: Registration of soil inputs will commence in 2026, following the operationalization of soil input business cases.

title.narrative: Output 2.1A wider variety of soil inputs produced by private sector and by small-scale entrepreneurs
2.1.3Number of soil input types produced and made available to small scale producers in selected woredas.

description.narrative: The number of distinct soil input products (e.g., compost, vermicompost, biochar, lime, biofertilizers) that are produced locally and made accessible for purchase or distribution to small-scale producers in targeted woredas.

comment.narrative: With program support, farmers are currently producing and applying two types of soil inputs—compost and vermicompost. Through capacity building trainings, technical guidance, and practical demonstrations, farmers have adopted these organic inputs to improve soil fertility and enhance sustainable land management practices.

title.narrative: 2.1.1 Number of business cases (Private sector partnerships) developed for production of soil inputs

description.narrative: The number of documented, structured business cases or partnership plans developed with private sector actors to support investment in producing soil inputs like compost, biofertilizer, lime, and organic amendments.

comment.narrative: In 2025, as preparation for business case development, the program conducted preliminary feasibility studies on selected organic inputs and soil amendments to assess production capacity, commercial viability, and agronomic benefits. The findings from these studies informed the development of structured business cases in 2026, aimed at reducing investment risk and providing a clear roadmap for entrepreneurs to scale within the market.

title.narrative: 2.1.2Private Sector investments in soil health products

description.narrative: The total monetary value (Euro) or number of confirmed private sector financial commitments directed toward producing, marketing, or distributing soil health products such as compost, biofertilizers, or lime.

comment.narrative: Reporting on private sector investment in soil input production will commence in 2026, once the business cases are finalized and begin to materialize.

title.narrative: Output 4.2Evidence base for policy analysis and regulatory support provided
4.2.3Subsidy program for agro-inputs and other policies and regulations assessed and recommendations for improvement formulated.

description.narrative: The number of formal assessments conducted of subsidy programs and other policies or regulations relevant to soil health, resulting in documented recommendations for policy improvements.

comment.narrative: The assessment of agro input subsidy programs, along with relevant policies and regulatory frameworks, is planned to commence in 2026.

title.narrative: 4.2.1Number of discussion papers and policy analysis developed for the Platform meetings

description.narrative: The number of formal discussion papers or policy analysis documents prepared to inform and guide stakeholder dialogue during national or regional soil health platform meetings.

comment.narrative: No discussion paper development was planned for 2025; however, platform mapping and assessments were conducted to inform the design and implementation of future discussion papers and engagement activities.

title.narrative: 4.2.2Number of meetings, conferences and web-based knowledge dissemination sessions held.

description.narrative: The total number of stakeholder meetings, conferences, webinars, or other knowledge-sharing events conducted to disseminate soil health and fertility information and support collaborative learning.

comment.narrative: During the reporting period, five conferences and meetings—two at the national level and three at the regional level—were facilitated, fully meeting the planned target for 2025.

title.narrative: Output 1.2.Collective action of small-scale producers and communities to restore and conserve soil health and fertility
1.2.3 Number of kebeles with a kebele vision for land management improvement.

description.narrative: The number of kebeles that have developed and endorsed a locally tailored strategic plan or vision document outlining collective priorities and actions for sustainable land management improvement.

comment.narrative: All 48 intervention kebeles have developed kebele level visions for land management and restoration as a result of successive trainings on participatory integrated planning.

title.narrative: 1.2.1 Number of small-scale food producers capacitated through producer-to-producer training (gender and age disaggregated)

description.narrative: The number of small-scale food producers who have gained new knowledge and skills in sustainable soil health and fertility practices through structured, peer-led training sessions, with results reported by gender and age.

comment.narrative: In the second half of 2025, 30 innovative farmers were selected from each of the 48 intervention kebeles and received training on Participatory Integrated Planning. These farmers are expected to serve as lead farmers and support producer to producer training, which is planned to commence in 2026.

title.narrative: 1.2.2 Number of woredas implement collective soil health and fertility extension practices.

description.narrative: The number of woredas where local authorities and extension services have officially adopted and implemented coordinated, community-based approaches to promote improved soil health and fertility management practices.

comment.narrative: Participatory Integrated Planning modules are currently being implemented in 12 woredas and 48 kebeles. In Ethiopia’s administrative structure, a kebele represents the lowest level of administration.

title.narrative: Output 4.1Information, data, and experiences on soil health and fertility shared among stakeholders
4.1.1.Number of soil health platforms adapted or established at national and regional levels.

description.narrative: The number of multi-stakeholder platforms created or modified at national or regional levels to facilitate regular dialogue, knowledge sharing, coordination, and joint planning on soil health and fertility management.

comment.narrative: One national and three regional multi stakeholder platform establishment workshops were conducted. These platforms are dedicated to addressing key challenges in the enabling environment for soil health and fertility management through coordinated dialogue, collaboration, and policy engagement among relevant stakeholders.

title.narrative: Outcome 3: Knowledge and evidence of best action research on integrated soil health and fertility practices is available, acceptable, and accessible for small-scale producers, including women and youth
3.2. Number of TVET students with hands-on experience in action research on soil health and fertility practices (disaggregated by gender)

description.narrative: The number of TVET students who gain practical experience through apprenticeship and/or conducting field-based action research on soil health and fertility management, tracked with gender-disaggregated data.

comment.narrative: In 2025, efforts focused on identifying context specific, farmer led action research agendas. Plans to engage students in action research are set for 2026, once research protocols are finalized and ready for implementation.

title.narrative: 3.1. Number of small-scale food producers conducting action research on their agricultural land (disaggregated by gender)

description.narrative: The number of small-scale producers actively engaged in testing, evaluating, and refining soil health and fertility practices on their own farms through structured, participatory research processes, with results reported by gender.

comment.narrative: In 2025, program efforts focused on identifying farmer driven action research priorities based on farmers’ needs. Accordingly, in 2026, context appropriate action research protocols will be developed for the implementation regions, and farmer led action research will be facilitated during the cropping season of the reporting year.

title.narrative: Output 3.2Strengthened data use and evidence base by project beneficiaries, partners and stakeholders
3.2.2Number of researchers capacitated in standardizing soil and fertilizer analysis, soil data collection and management.

description.narrative: The number of researchers trained to apply standardized methods for soil and fertilizer analysis, as well as best practices in soil data collection, management, and interpretation to support evidence-based recommendations.

comment.narrative: A total of 53 researchers were capacitated in soil data collection and management. The training focused on soil profile description using the World Reference Base (WRB) classification system and digital data collection using Open Data Kit (ODK) tools.

title.narrative: 3.2.1 Number of small-scale producers using the Decision Support Tool for ISFM and fertilizers (as part of the pilot)

description.narrative: The number of small-scale producers who have been trained and actively use the Decision Support Tool to inform their Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM) and fertilizer application decisions in pilot areas.

comment.narrative: Farmers’ utilization of the Decision Support Tool (DST) was not planned for 2025. Utilization is planned for 2026, once DST calibration is finalized and farmers receive the required training.

title.narrative: 1.Farmland is converted to sustainable use.
1.1Hectares of farmland converted to sustainable use

description.narrative: The total area of agricultural land that has been transitioned from conventional or unsustainable farming methods into socially acceptable, economically viable and environmentally sustainable uses. This includes regenerative, and climate-resilient agricultural practices, agroecological farming, soil and water conservation and integrated soil fertility management (ISFM).

comment.narrative: An impact-level indicator, measurement is not expected during the first year, as changes at this level require a longer time frame to materialize.

title.narrative: Outcome 1. Small-scale producers and communities are empowered to become resilient and stewards of their agricultural land.
1.3Number of watersheds supported with land management practices.

description.narrative: The number of watershed areas and restoration sites where sustainable land management interventions have been implemented to prevent soil erosion, enhance water retention, and restore ecosystem balance. These practices may include terracing, reforestation, gully rehabilitation, agroforestry, and community-based watershed management efforts, contributing to improved agricultural productivity, climate resilience, and sustainable livelihoods.

comment.narrative: In 2025, program efforts focused on identifying and mapping watersheds and land degradation hotspots targeted for restoration. As a result, restoration and land management support activities will commence in 2026, ahead of the start of the rainy season.

title.narrative: 1.1Number of farm households effectively integrate soil health and fertility practices on their farm (gender and age disaggregated)

description.narrative: The number of farming households adopting sustainable soil management practices, such as composting, crop rotation, agroforestry, vertisol management and organic fertilizers, to maintain soil fertility and productivity. This indicator tracks adoption rates while considering gender and age to ensure inclusivity in sustainable agriculture initiatives.

comment.narrative: In 2025, farmers were enrolled in various capacity building trainings and received advisory services. As a result, the implementation of integrated practices on farmers’ plots is expected to be realized during the 2026 cropping season.

title.narrative: 1.2Number of hectares of farmland with (at least two) integrated conservation practices mainstreamed in targeted kebeles (directly and indirectly reached)

description.narrative: Total area of agricultural land where at least two sustainable land management practices—such as terracing, agroforestry, crop rotation, mulching, or water harvesting—have been implemented and institutionalized within specific kebeles. This includes both directly influenced by project interventions and indirectly impacted through farmer-to-farmer knowledge transfer and policy adoption, contributing to improved soil health, water retention, and climate resilience.

comment.narrative: In 2025, the focus was on building farmers’ capacity to design integrated plot plans. These plans will be implemented on farmers’ plots during the 2026 cropping season. Therefore, reporting on the hectares of farmland under at least two integrated practices will commence in 2026.
